opus-5.5.text:
I think they're actually some of the most valuable people you can have on a post-training team, and honestly they're often undervalued.

Post-training isn't really about running a fixed recipe. It's about knowing where the model falls short, what "good" looks like, and how to close that gap. People who spend a lot of time just playing with models, pushing them, trying weird prompts, comparing versions, build up an intuition you can't get from benchmark numbers. They can tell you, "this model feels smart on math but it's brittle when the instructions get long," or "it's technically correct but the tone is off," or "it gives up too early on hard agentic tasks." That kind of qualitative sense is exactly what tells you which data to build and which capabilities to prioritize next.

I'd say they contribute in a few concrete ways. First, finding failure modes. A lot of the most important problems were never captured by any eval, and someone had to stumble on them through hands-on use. Second, designing data and evals. Once you've felt a weakness, you can turn it into a targeted dataset or a new evaluation, and that often matters more than tweaking the algorithm. Third, taste. In the end post-training is shaping a model's behavior and personality, and someone has to judge whether a response is actually good, not just whether it scores well. People who've talked to many models have much better calibration there.

So my view is that strong post-training teams need both sides: people with solid engineering and algorithm skills, and people with a sharp, almost user-like sensitivity to model behavior. Ideally the same person has both. The ones who keep exploring capabilities are often the first to see where the next breakthrough or the next problem is coming from.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're actually one of the most underrated sources of signal for post-training, and let me explain why.

When you do post-training, the hard part is almost never the algorithm. The hard part is knowing what "good" looks like. You need to know where the model is weak, what kinds of prompts expose that weakness, and what a genuinely better answer would be. People who spend all day poking at models have a kind of intuition about the model's behavior that's very hard to get from benchmarks. They notice that the model gets lazy on long reasoning chains, or that it over-hedges on certain questions, or that it fails in a specific way when the instruction has two constraints that conflict. These are exactly the failure modes that a static eval set won't catch, because the eval was built before anyone knew the model would fail that way.

So concretely, I think there are three ways they contribute. First, they generate hard cases. A good prompt that reliably breaks the model is worth more than a thousand easy ones, because it tells you precisely where the boundary of capability is. Second, they help define the reward signal. If you're doing RL, whether with a reward model or with rule-based verification, someone has to decide what counts as a good response, and people with deep experience using models often have better taste about that than people writing the training code. Third, they close the loop. After you ship a new checkpoint, these people are the first to tell you whether the change actually helped or whether you just moved the failure somewhere else.

What I'd say to those people is: don't just share screenshots of funny mistakes. Try to characterize the failure. Is it reproducible? What's the minimal prompt that triggers it? Does it go away if you rephrase? That kind of structured observation is basically free data for a post-training team, and it's the kind of data we're always short of.

astra-6.text:
I think they can contribute a lot, because they develop an intuition for where a model is strong and where it still falls short. They notice things that a benchmark score might miss: an answer that looks convincing but doesn’t solve the problem, or a task the model can handle only if you phrase the prompt very carefully.

The key is to turn that intuition into concrete feedback. Can you give a reproducible example? Can you explain what makes the response inadequate and what a better response would look like? Is it an isolated failure, or does it happen across a whole category of tasks? Those observations can help us build better training examples and evaluations.

I’d also want those people involved throughout the process. After a round of post-training, let them explore again: did we actually improve the capability, or did we just make the responses sound better? That feedback loop is very valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they can contribute a lot, because post-training depends on understanding the gap between what a model can do and what it actually does in practice. People who spend a lot of time exploring models often develop a very good intuition for that gap. They notice when a model needs a particular prompt to solve something, when it gives up too early, or when an answer sounds convincing but doesn’t really address the question.

The key is to turn those observations into concrete examples. What was the task? What did the model do? What would a better response look like? Can you reproduce the failure across different prompts? Those examples can become training data or evaluations, and they can help us tell whether a change actually improves the model.

So I wouldn’t see these people simply as testers at the end of the process. They can help define what we should train for in the first place. That practical understanding of model behavior is a very valuable contribution to post-training.
